task.goal: Reduce mislabeled samples in a small soil-testing lab during handoffs.
hard_constraints: Two technicians process 40 samples daily with printed labels and one shared spreadsheet; no barcode purchase.
Original samples and identifiers must remain traceable; do not relabel from memory.
Measure wrong labels, handoff time and unresolved mismatches over two weeks.
task.available_resources: Existing intake forms and last month's correction log.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Source-checked handoff with explicit acceptance
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make each transfer a short, two-person verification. The sender presents the sample and its intake form; the receiver independently reads the identifier on the sample and compares it with the form and the corresponding spreadsheet row before accepting custody. This changes the handoff from an assumed transfer into an explicit check against the original record, potentially catching transpositions and transfers to the wrong row.

Add columns to the shared spreadsheet for sender, receiver, transfer time and status: accepted or mismatch pending. Only one technician edits the transfer record at a time. For a mismatch, retain the sample, existing label and intake form together in a designated hold area. Record the conflicting identifiers verbatim. Resolve using documentary evidence; preserve the original entry and append any correction, its evidence, date and technician. Never replace an identifier from memory.

Use last month's correction log to select the most error-prone handoff for the first trial. The procedure needs no new equipment, but both technicians must overlap briefly at that handoff. It assumes the intake form is a reliable reference; matching errors already present on both form and label may escape detection. The additional coordination could also outweigh the benefit if errors mainly originate elsewhere. Reversal consists of removing the acceptance requirement while retaining all traceability records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across two weeks, alternate ordinary and verified handoffs by predetermined half-days, balancing morning and afternoon periods. Keep mismatch containment and measurement identical in both conditions. Record confirmed wrong-label events per sample, elapsed handoff seconds and unresolved mismatches at each day's end, including their age. Apply the same end-of-batch source audit to both conditions and count each error once. Inspect a few transfers first to confirm that the receiver actually checks the source independently. The mechanism is challenged if checks are routinely skipped, wrong-label rates do not improve, or delay and unresolved work increase substantially. With only 40 samples daily, report counts and uncertainty rather than claiming proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Fixed-position custody with a traveling manifest
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep samples in numbered positions within an existing rack, tray or clearly marked bench area, and hand over the entire group with a position manifest. Each position maps to an original sample identifier copied from the intake form and checked against the printed sample label before loading. The primary mechanism is physical separation and stable placement: technicians need fewer loose-sample transfers in which labels, forms or neighboring samples can become confused.

Record batch, position, original identifier, current custodian and exceptions in a separate spreadsheet tab. A position number is only a location reference, never a replacement sample identifier. Keep each existing sample label intact and retain the intake forms with the batch. At handoff, the receiver checks occupied positions, vacancies and manifest agreement before accepting the group. If processing requires removal, mark the position out; return the sample only after checking its original identifier. Hold unexplained discrepancies without guessing or silently moving samples to make the manifest fit.

Use the correction log to identify whether swaps between neighboring samples or lost batch membership are plausible targets. Prerequisites are sufficient existing space and a workflow that permits samples to stay in assigned positions through at least one handoff. This may offer little benefit where samples must constantly change containers or where labels are already wrong at intake. Positions can also create false confidence, so the manifest cannot substitute for checking identifiers. The procedure is reversible by retiring the location mapping after all samples are reconciled.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, allocate comparable batches by a predetermined alternating sequence to fixed-position handling or current handling. Record confirmed wrong labels, handoff duration and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages for both. Use the same source audit after handoff in both groups. Before live use, conduct a paper-only rehearsal with an intentionally incorrect manifest position; check whether the receiver detects it without relying on location alone. No live sample is deliberately mislabeled. Reject or revise the approach if position records frequently become stale, swaps persist, or maintaining the manifest takes longer than the transfer errors it prevents justify. Interpret low error counts cautiously.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One-sample labeling gate before transfer
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Prevent labels from being assigned to the wrong sample by allowing only one sample, its intake form and its matching printed label in the active labeling area at a time. Complete that sample's label application and source check before bringing the next sample into the area. Keep unused printed labels separate from completed samples. The primary mechanism is reducing opportunities for cross-assignment during preparation, before a handoff exposes the mistake.

Review last month's correction log to identify the step where labels are first applied or a labeled derivative is created. Introduce the gate there. Add spreadsheet fields for source identifier, labeling completion and next custodian. Check the printed identifier against the intake form and the sample's existing identifier before marking completion. For derivatives, record the parent identifier and retain the parent-to-derivative relationship. Never cover or discard an original identifier to make a discrepancy disappear. Isolate unexpected or duplicate labels, preserve the conflicting evidence and append documented corrections rather than overwriting history.

The receiving technician accepts only samples marked complete and checks that each physical sample has a corresponding spreadsheet entry. This requires an existing surface that can be kept clear and enough discipline to avoid overlapping labeling tasks. It assumes label cross-assignment is a meaningful source of errors; it will not reliably catch an incorrect identifier already printed consistently across all source documents. Frequent interruptions may reduce throughput. Reversal simply restores the previous preparation sequence while retaining all completed tracking and correction records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Over two weeks, use a predetermined alternating schedule of ordinary preparation and one-sample preparation, with equal coverage of each technician where feasible. Keep receiving checks and end-of-batch audits identical. Record confirmed wrong-label events per sample, handoff seconds and daily unresolved mismatches with their age; also record preparation time to expose any shifted workload. Rehearse with spare paper identifiers to inspect whether an interruption leaves an unambiguous active sample and label. The proposal is weakened if multiple samples accumulate in the active area, label errors remain unchanged, or preparation delays grow without an observable reduction in mismatches. Treat a zero-error fortnight as limited evidence, not proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Keep one technician responsible from intake to completion
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Replace routine transfers of partly processed samples with end-to-end responsibility. Assign each incoming sample to one of the two technicians in the shared spreadsheet; that technician performs its processing and closes its record. Both technicians continue working, but divide samples rather than dividing processing stages. The mechanism is reducing the number of custody changes where a sample can become associated with another sample's label or spreadsheet row.

First inspect the intake forms and last month's correction log to identify a processing route both technicians can complete. Apply ownership to that route, balancing assignments by expected workload rather than assuming every sample takes equal effort. Shared equipment can still be scheduled between technicians without transferring sample responsibility. Preserve all printed labels and original identifiers. Record owner, processing status and any unavoidable transfer in the existing spreadsheet, with one editor at a time.

For an unexpected mismatch, pause that sample, retain its label and intake documentation, and record conflicting identifiers verbatim. Resolve only from documentary evidence, appending the correction and its basis without deleting the original record. Never relabel from memory. If an owner becomes unavailable, record an explicit exception transfer rather than allowing unrecorded substitution.

This requires both technicians to be qualified for the selected route and equipment scheduling that permits individual responsibility. It may worsen queues where specialization is essential, and it cannot prevent mistakes already present at intake. Reversal restores stage-based assignments while retaining ownership and correction records.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: For two weeks, assign comparable eligible batches by a predetermined alternating sequence to individual ownership or current stage-based handling. Give both groups the same final comparison against intake records. Record confirmed wrong-label counts and sample denominators, total handoff seconds per batch, seconds per actual handoff, and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages. Record completion time to expose displaced delays. A batch with no transfer has zero total handoff time; its per-handoff time is not applicable. Inspect the first day's records: if ownership does not reduce actual transfers, its mechanism has failed. Revise or reject it if errors persist or queues materially worsen. Low error counts will leave effectiveness uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Spreadsheet reconciliation that exposes duplicate and missing identifiers
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the shared spreadsheet to flag impossible or incomplete handoff records automatically. The mechanism is a consistency check across the whole batch: assigning the same identifier to two containers should also leave another expected identifier missing. This can expose errors that remain unnoticed when technicians inspect samples individually.

Create a trial tab containing the expected identifiers from existing intake forms, preserving the original records. For each handoff, the receiving technician enters the identifier actually visible on each container into a separate observed column, formatted as text to preserve leading zeros. Use ordinary spreadsheet formulas or conditional formatting to flag unexpected identifiers, repeated identifiers and expected samples without a receipt. Do not populate observed identifiers automatically from the expected list. Process one editor at a time.

First establish whether identifiers uniquely identify containers. Where legitimate derivatives share a parent identifier, reconcile their documented container identifiers or expected multiplicities separately; do not invent replacement identities. Keep original labels intact. Hold flagged samples with their intake documentation, record conflicting values verbatim, and append evidence-backed resolutions without overwriting the original observation. Never relabel from memory.

This requires spreadsheet functions already available and time to enter observed identifiers. It assumes duplicate, omitted or unexpected identifiers explain some errors in last month's correction log. A complete swap between two valid identifiers will pass reconciliation, and typing mistakes can create false alarms. Reversal consists of disabling the trial checks while retaining the observations and correction history.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
First test the formulas on copied historical or fictional rows containing a duplicate, an omission and an unexpected identifier; also include a valid two-sample swap to demonstrate the limitation. Do not alter live labels.

Across two weeks, alternate comparable batches between reconciliation and ordinary recording. Apply the same final intake-document audit to both. Record confirmed wrong-label counts and sample totals, handoff seconds including data entry, and daily unresolved mismatch counts and ages. Distinguish transcription alarms from physical label errors. Inspect whether flags appear before samples advance. Frequent false alarms, ignored flags or unchanged audited errors would challenge usefulness; few errors would leave effectiveness uncertain.

EXPAND.title: Keep spreadsheet identity fixed while work status changes
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent handoff errors caused by editing, sorting or selecting the wrong spreadsheet record. Unlike source-checked acceptance, which depends on both technicians being available and noticing a discrepancy, this route constrains how the shared record can change. It is useful only if spreadsheet mistakes contribute to physical mislabeling or apparent sample swaps; last month's correction log should establish whether that is plausible.

At intake, one technician enters the identifier exactly as printed on the intake form, preserving leading zeros, and checks it against the existing sample label. Keep the original intake forms. Use one table with fixed identifier and intake-reference columns, editable processing-status fields, and a separate append-only correction sheet. Use existing spreadsheet protection and duplicate highlighting if supported; otherwise this route loses much of its preventive value. Sort only complete table rows. Protect identity cells against routine editing and prohibit using row numbers as sample identities.

At handoff, the receiving technician finds the physical sample's printed identifier in the table and records custody in that record. Missing or duplicate matches trigger a hold, with conflicting identifiers recorded verbatim. A designated technician makes any evidence-supported correction by adding a dated correction record while preserving the original entry and label. Neither technician may infer a replacement identifier from memory. Disable protection to reverse the procedure, retaining the records.

This needs existing spreadsheet features and a short setup session, not new equipment. It cannot prevent a correctly recorded label being attached to the wrong container, and protection is an accidental-error barrier rather than a secure audit trail.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician A owns a two-week trial of approximately 400 samples, assuming ten working days. Assign comparable batches in advance to constrained spreadsheet handling or the prior source-checked acceptance procedure. Keep discrepancy containment and final intake-form audits identical. Count confirmed wrong labels per sample, handoff seconds, daily unresolved mismatches and their ages; also record spreadsheet administration time and physical samples held because records cannot be found. First inspect a disposable copy using a duplicate identifier and attempted identity edit. Stop the trial arm if an original identifier becomes unrecoverable or a spreadsheet restriction prevents safe custody recording. Prefer the prior route if errors are no lower and total handling time or holds increase. Sparse errors may leave the comparison inconclusive.

EXPAND.title: Retire surplus labels through a label inventory
EXPAND.proposal:
Remove obsolete and duplicate printed labels before they can be attached to another sample. The working principle is controlling the supply of plausible but incorrect labels, rather than changing sample placement or adding a two-person transfer check.

At intake, Technician A records each original sample identifier and the number of printed labels available for it in a label-control tab of the existing spreadsheet. Check those identifiers against intake forms before releasing labels for use. Keep loose labels with their matching intake paperwork. Whenever a label is applied, record its intended container or derivative relationship. Retain original sample identifiers and labels; this procedure does not authorize replacing them.

Before handing over a batch, the sender reconciles printed labels into applied, unused or void categories. Unused and void labels remain attached to their intake paperwork and are clearly marked against further use without obscuring their identifiers. Record a reprint and its reason before introducing it into circulation. The receiver checks that no unaccounted loose labels accompany the batch and records custody against the original identifiers.

A missing label, unexpected extra or unexplained reprint triggers a hold on the affected samples and labels. Resolve it from intake forms and documented processing records, preserving conflicting evidence and appending corrections. Counts alone never establish that labels were attached correctly.

This requires spare space on existing forms and spreadsheet entries. It assumes surplus labels or reprints are a credible source of mistakes, which the correction log may or may not support. It could add paperwork without helping if all errors arise from exchanging two valid labels. Reversal ends label accounting after outstanding inventories have been reconciled; retain all history.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician B owns a two-week trial, alternating comparable batches between label inventory and ordinary label handling. Both receive the same final source audit and mismatch containment. Measure confirmed wrong labels per sample, elapsed handoff time and end-of-day unresolved mismatches with age. Record label-accounting time separately to reveal work shifted before handoff. Start with paper-only reconciliation containing one unexplained extra label; failure to detect it challenges feasibility. Stop if inventory work causes unattended samples or if labels are retired without preserving readable identifiers. Reject or simplify the procedure if wrong-label counts do not improve while total handling time rises. Distinguish inventory discrepancies from confirmed wrong labels.

EXPAND.title: Keep one technician responsible for each sample through processing
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce opportunities for mislabeling by removing avoidable changes of custodian. Each technician owns assigned samples from intake through processing and final release, instead of routinely exchanging partly processed samples. This changes the division of work rather than the checking ritual at each transfer.

Use last month's correction log and the current workflow to identify transfers that exist for convenience rather than equipment access or required review. At intake, assign samples in a predetermined alternating sequence, balancing known processing demands where possible. Record owner and original identifier in the shared spreadsheet, checked against the intake form and existing label. Each owner completes the steps they are qualified to perform and records derivative-to-parent relationships when applicable. Existing labels and intake records remain intact.

Use shared equipment in scheduled turns while custody stays with the owner where practical. A genuine custody change still requires a recorded sender, receiver, time and original identifier. The receiver checks the sample against its intake record. Any discrepancy places the affected material on hold; preserve both identifiers and resolve only from documentary evidence, appending corrections rather than overwriting history.

The decision boundary is operational: retain ownership when the assigned technician can safely complete the next step within the lab's existing time requirements; transfer when qualification, absence or a documented processing deadline requires it. Ownership must never justify skipping a required independent review.

This needs both technicians to be qualified for most steps and enough flexibility around shared equipment. Those prerequisites are unconfirmed. It can reduce transfer opportunities but may increase queues, reduce specialization benefits or let one person's intake mistake persist. Reverse it by returning to task-based assignments after recording custody of every open sample.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician A owns a bounded two-week comparison: alternate whole days between continuous ownership and ordinary task-based allocation, balancing weekdays where feasible. Apply the same final intake-form audit and mismatch recovery in both conditions. Record actual custody changes, confirmed wrong labels per sample, handoff seconds and daily unresolved mismatches with age. Also measure completion delays and overtime, since fewer handoffs could conceal a throughput cost. Inspect the first day's records to confirm that ownership reflects actual handling. Stop continuous ownership if a required processing deadline or independent review is jeopardized. If transfers fall but wrong labels do not, the mechanism may target the wrong source of error; if error counts are low throughout, report uncertainty rather than claiming success.

EXPAND.title: Improved P0: Source-checked handoff with recorded pending custody
EXPAND.proposal:
This retains P0’s mechanism: the receiver checks the physical identifier against the original intake form before accepting custody. The substantive change is explicit handling of unavailable receivers and pending transfers, removing the assumption that both technicians can always overlap.

At preparation, check the original sample identifier against its intake form and locate its spreadsheet record. Preserve existing labels and record parent identifiers for derivatives. The sender records the identifier, intended receiver, placement and dispatch time, then places the sample with its paperwork in an existing designated pending area. Custody remains with the sender until acceptance; placement alone does not transfer responsibility.

The receiver independently compares the sample label, intake form and spreadsheet record, then records acceptance and time. No processing starts while acceptance is pending. Record conflicting identifiers verbatim, retain the material and documentation together, and resolve discrepancies only through documentary evidence. Append corrections with their evidence and author; preserve original identifiers and entries.

This needs an existing separable bench area, several spreadsheet columns and sequential spreadsheet editing. Intake records must be sufficiently reliable; agreement cannot reveal an error repeated throughout the records. If secure pending placement or delayed processing is unsuitable, use P0’s simultaneous check at a scheduled handoff. Urgent work must use that fallback rather than bypass acceptance. Ending pending transfers and returning to simultaneous checks reverses the change while preserving records.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician A coordinates a ten-working-day trial; both technicians perform acceptance. Alternate comparable daily batches between original P0 and this version, retaining the same documentary check. Use last month’s correction log to define error categories before starting. Record confirmed wrong-label samples per samples handled, active handoff time, elapsed dispatch-to-acceptance time, and unresolved mismatches at each day’s end. Distinguish discovered pre-existing errors from errors introduced during the trial. Inspect the first pending batch before continuing. Stop asynchronous transfers after any unaccepted sample is processed or a pending transfer breaches an existing processing deadline; use simultaneous acceptance thereafter. Equal error counts with longer waiting or more unresolved mismatches would show no practical gain. Rare errors and the short trial limit conclusions.

EXPAND.title: Prevent identifier loss during wet and dirty handling
EXPAND.proposal:
Target a different failure mechanism: an initially correct printed label becomes obscured, detached or unreadable during soil processing, prompting later misidentification. Review last month’s correction log and existing labels for evidence of this pathway before selecting the trial. Its contribution is currently unknown.

At entry, verify the original printed identifier against the intake form and record any existing damage. Before each wet or dirty operation, position the container so the label avoids the expected contact surface, keep paperwork in a dry part of the existing work area, and avoid placing labeled surfaces against wet benches or soil. Use existing labeling materials and handling space; do not introduce unverified coatings, sleeves or cleaning chemicals. Never obscure an original identifier.

After exposure and before handoff, inspect whether the identifier remains readable and attached. Record deterioration in the spreadsheet immediately. This inspection detects physical degradation; it cannot establish that a readable label belongs to the correct sample. Continue the lab’s existing identity checks.

If an identifier becomes uncertain, stop processing that sample and preserve its label, container and intake paperwork. A replacement is allowed only when contemporaneous documentary evidence uniquely connects that container to its original identifier. Retain the old label or a documented transcription of its surviving content and append the correction. Otherwise leave the mismatch unresolved on hold.

The prerequisite is a handling step where contact can be avoided without compromising the test or worker safety. Where avoidance is impossible with existing resources, retain the established method and inspect immediately afterward. If damage is absent from the log and initial observations, do not expand this route. Reversal restores prior handling while retaining damage and correction records.
EXPAND.experiment: Technician B owns a two-week trial on one applicable processing step. Alternate comparable batches between existing handling and contact-avoiding handling, with the same inspection in both groups. Across all 40 daily samples, record confirmed wrong labels, handoff time and end-of-day unresolved mismatches; additionally count newly damaged labels and processing delays. Inspect the first treated batch for interference with testing. Stop altered handling if it compromises safe handling, test requirements or an existing processing deadline. No reduction in damage or wrong labels, especially with longer handoffs or more holds, would falsify its practical value. Improved readability alone would not establish reduced mislabeling.
